title: What Luel's contributor network makes possible
summary: A global contributor network gives us the reach to collect data around the people, languages and conditions a model needs to understand.
body_markdown:
At Luel, more than 900,000 contributors across 96+ countries complete audio, video and image tasks. Behind that number are people speaking different languages, using different devices and recording in the places they live. That range matters because the data a model needs is often specific: a regional dialect, a conversation recorded on a phone, or an everyday task seen from the person doing it. Building a network gives us a way to collect those examples deliberately.


## More people, broader coverage


A dataset can contain thousands of hours and still draw from a small group of speakers. More recordings from those people add volume, but leave other accents, speaking habits and environments unrepresented. The same problem appears in video and images, where a large collection can repeatedly show the same places and ways of doing things.


A broader contributor base gives collection more room to reflect that variation. For speech, this can mean reaching speakers from different regions, capturing everyday language alongside formal speech, or collecting across different microphones and rooms. Each choice changes what the dataset covers and what we can reasonably expect a model trained on it to handle.


The total network size does not tell us how many suitable contributors are available for every task. Each collection still needs a defined brief and the right participants. It gives us a larger starting point for finding them.


## Collecting what is missing


For some projects, an existing dataset is enough. Others need recordings that are difficult to find in a public corpus or a commercial catalog. A team may need a particular spoken dialect, more independent speakers, or examples from the conditions where its product struggles.


A contributor network makes it possible to organize collection around that need. The language, task and recording conditions can be set before the data is created, with acceptance criteria that match its intended use.


Our speech work shows why this matters. The native-speaker corpora behind our Masri, Darija, Tibetan and Dzongkha voices connect collection directly to model development. Speakers contribute the language a voice needs to learn, including pronunciation and everyday usage that a broad language label can overlook. That work is part of the research program at[Luel Labs](https://www.luel.ai/lab) .


## Improving the next collection


Data needs also change as a model develops. An initial collection may support a first version, while testing reveals that it struggles with a certain accent or recording condition. Those findings give the next collection a more precise purpose.


Having an established network lets us build on the collection process as those needs change. We can use what we learn from a model to shape the next task, then evaluate whether the additional data helped. The value extends beyond the first dataset to the ability to keep addressing gaps as they become clear.


## Reach needs quality control


At Luel, contributors are paid per accepted submission. Every submission is consented, and speech runs through quality assurance before anything downstream can use it. The collection brief decides what counts as usable: a first-person video only works if the hands stay in frame for the whole action, and a conversation only works if every speaker can be heard.


Growing the network expands who we can reach. Clear tasks and quality checks turn that reach into usable data. Together, they give us a way to build datasets around the people and conditions our models need to serve, and to keep improving that coverage as we learn.
